name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Excretory structures across diverse animal groups

questiontext.text:
Match the excretory structures in Column I with their representative animals in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Protonephridia I. Prawn
B. Nephridia II. Cockroach
C. Malpighian tubules III. Planaria
D. Antennal glands IV. Earthworm

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different animal phyla have evolved specialized excretory structures adapted to their physiological needs for nitrogenous waste elimination and osmoregulation.

Step 2: Structures in Platyhelminthes and Annelids
Protonephridia, or flame cells, are primitive tubular excretory organs primarily concerned with osmoregulation in flatworms like Planaria, rotifers, some annelids, and cephalochordates. Nephridia are coiled tubular structures found in earthworms and other annelids that eliminate metabolic wastes and maintain fluid volume.

Step 3: Structures in Arthropods
Malpighian tubules are characteristic filamentous excretory organs found in insects including cockroaches. Antennal glands, also called green glands, perform excretory and osmoregulatory roles in crustaceans such as prawns.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Protonephridia with Planaria, Nephridia with Earthworm, Malpighian tubules with Cockroach, and Antennal glands with Prawn.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Modes of excretion and animal representatives

questiontext.text:
Match the excretory nature or organism in Column I with the correct description or category in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Ammonotelism I. Protonephridia
B. Terrestrial amphibians II. Uricotelism
C. Reptiles and birds III. Many bony fishes
D. Cephalochordate Amphioxus IV. Ureotelism

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The nature of nitrogenous waste excreted by an animal depends largely on water availability and habitat, dividing animals into ammonotelic, ureotelic, and uricotelic forms.

Step 2: Analysis of Ammonotelism and Ureotelism
Ammonotelism is observed in aquatic organisms such as many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, and aquatic insects where ammonia readily diffuses across body or gill surfaces. Terrestrial adaptations led to ureotelism in mammals, many terrestrial amphibians, and marine fishes, converting ammonia to less toxic urea in the liver.

Step 3: Analysis of Uricotelism and Primitive Excretory Units
Reptiles, birds, land snails, and insects excrete uric acid as pellets or paste with minimal water loss, exhibiting uricotelism. Amphioxus is a cephalochordate that relies on protonephridia for osmoregulation and ionic balance.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Ammonotelism with Many bony fishes, Terrestrial amphibians with Ureotelism, Reptiles and birds with Uricotelism, and Cephalochordate Amphioxus with Protonephridia.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Segments of nephron and their functions

questiontext.text:
Match the segments of the human nephron in Column I with their primary functional attributes in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Proximal convoluted tubule I. Permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes
B. Descending limb of Henle's loop II. Conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water
C. Ascending limb of Henle's loop III. Reabsorption of 70 to 80 percent of electrolytes and water
D. Distal convoluted tubule IV. Impermeable to water but allows active or passive transport of electrolytes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different segments of the nephron possess specialized epithelial linings that determine differential permeability to water and electrolytes.

Step 2: Convoluted Tubule Functions
The proximal convoluted tubule is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium that increases surface area, reabsorbing nearly all essential nutrients along with 70 to 80 percent of electrolytes and water. The distal convoluted tubule carries out conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water regulated by hormones.

Step 3: Permeability of Henle's Loop Limbs
The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, leading to concentration of the filtrate as it descends. The ascending limb is impermeable to water but allows active or passive transport of electrolytes, diluting the filtrate as it ascends.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Proximal convoluted tubule with reabsorption of 70 to 80 percent of electrolytes and water, Descending limb of Henle's loop with permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, Ascending limb of Henle's loop with impermeable to water but allows active or passive transport of electrolytes, and Distal convoluted tubule with conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Hormonal regulators of human kidney function

questiontext.text:
Match the regulatory hormones or factors in Column I with their specific physiological actions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Antidiuretic hormone I. Converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I
B. Renin II. Causes vasodilation and checks renin-angiotensin mechanism
C. Aldosterone III. Facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule
D. Atrial natriuretic factor IV. Stimulates reabsorption of sodium ions and water from distal tubule

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kidney function is regulated by integrated feedback loops involving the hypothalamus, juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), adrenal cortex, and the heart.

Step 2: Hypothalamic and JGA Mediators
Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), released from the neurohypophysis in response to hyperosmolarity or fluid loss, acts on the latter parts of the tubule to promote water reabsorption and prevent diuresis. A decline in glomerular blood flow or pressure triggers juxtaglomerular cells to secrete renin, which converts circulating angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

Step 3: Adrenal and Cardiac Regulators
Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which drives reabsorption of sodium ions and water from distal renal tubules. In response to high atrial blood flow, the heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor, which causes vasodilation, lowers blood pressure, and antagonizes the renin-angiotensin pathway.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Antidiuretic hormone with facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule, Renin with converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I, Aldosterone with stimulates reabsorption of sodium ions and water from distal tubule, and Atrial natriuretic factor with causes vasodilation and checks renin-angiotensin mechanism.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Clinical disorders of the excretory system

questiontext.text:
Match the clinical conditions and disorders in Column I with their correct descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Uremia I. Inflammation of the glomeruli of kidney
B. Renal calculi II. Presence of glucose in urine indicating diabetes mellitus
C. Glomerulonephritis III. Accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction
D. Glycosuria IV. Insoluble mass of crystallised salts like oxalates formed within the kidney

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Excretory system malfunctions and metabolic imbalances produce specific clinical syndromes and diagnostic urinalysis findings.

Step 2: Renal Pathologies
Uremia occurs when kidney failure causes accumulation of urea in the blood, necessitating hemodialysis or renal transplantation. Renal calculi refer to stones or insoluble crystalline masses of salts, such as oxalates, formed inside the kidney. Glomerulonephritis is an inflammatory disease affecting the glomeruli of the kidneys.

Step 3: Urinalysis Indicators
The excretion of glucose in urine is termed glycosuria, which, when accompanied by ketone bodies (ketonuria), is a clinical hallmark of diabetes mellitus.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Uremia with accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction, Renal calculi with insoluble mass of crystallised salts like oxalates formed within the kidney, Glomerulonephritis with inflammation of the glomeruli of kidney, and Glycosuria with presence of glucose in urine indicating diabetes mellitus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Accessory excretory organs and eliminated substances

questiontext.text:
Match the accessory excretory organs or glands in Column I with their characteristic excretory secretions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Lungs I. Sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes in sebum
B. Liver II. Watery fluid containing sodium chloride, small amounts of urea, and lactic acid
C. Sweat glands III. Elimination of approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per minute
D. Sebaceous glands IV. Secretion containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, and degraded steroid hormones

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apart from kidneys, organs such as the lungs, liver, and skin assist significantly in excreting volatile, lipid-soluble, or metabolic wastes from the human body.

Step 2: Internal Excretory Organs
Human lungs eliminate approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per minute along with water vapor. The liver secretes bile pigments including bilirubin and biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins, and drugs that are eliminated with digestive feces.

Step 3: Cutaneous Glands
Sweat glands produce a watery solution containing sodium chloride, traces of urea, and lactic acid, serving primary cooling and secondary excretory roles. Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes via sebum, creating a protective oily skin coating.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Lungs with elimination of approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per minute, Liver with secretion containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, and degraded steroid hormones, Sweat glands with watery fluid containing sodium chloride, small amounts of urea, and lactic acid, and Sebaceous glands with sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes in sebum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - Structural components of human kidney anatomy

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical structures of the human kidney in Column I with their precise anatomical features in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Hilum I. Broad funnel-shaped space with calyces inner to the hilum
B. Renal pelvis II. Cortical tissue extending between medullary pyramids
C. Columns of Bertini III. Notch on inner concave surface where ureter, vessels, and nerves enter
D. Podocytes IV. Specialized epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule with filtration slits

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human kidney contains distinct macroscopic landmarks and microscopic cellular adaptations facilitating blood entry, filtration, and urine collection.

Step 2: Gross Anatomical Architecture
The hilum is a notch on the medial concave surface through which the ureter, renal blood vessels, and nerves pass. Directly inner to the hilum lies the renal pelvis, a broad funnel-shaped chamber with calyces collecting urine from medullary pyramids. The renal cortex projects inward between adjacent medullary pyramids as the Columns of Bertini.

Step 3: Microscopic Epithelial Architecture
Podocytes are complex epithelial cells of the inner visceral wall of Bowman's capsule that form filtration slits (slit pores) to permit fine ultrafiltration of plasma.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Hilum with notch on inner concave surface where ureter, vessels, and nerves enter, Renal pelvis with broad funnel-shaped space with calyces inner to the hilum, Columns of Bertini with cortical tissue extending between medullary pyramids, and Podocytes with specialized epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule with filtration slits.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Countercurrent mechanisms and medullary concentration gradient

questiontext.text:
Match the components of the countercurrent mechanism in Column I with their specific solute transport roles in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Ascending limb of Henle's loop I. Returns sodium chloride back to the medullary interstitium
B. Descending limb of vasa recta II. Allows small amounts of urea into medullary interstitium to maintain osmolarity
C. Ascending limb of vasa recta III. Transports sodium chloride that is exchanged with descending limb of vasa recta
D. Collecting duct IV. Takes up sodium chloride from medullary interstitium as blood flows downward

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The countercurrent multiplier system of Henle's loop and exchanger system of vasa recta maintain an osmolar gradient increasing from \(300\text{ mOsmol L}^{-1}\) in the cortex to \(1200\text{ mOsmol L}^{-1}\) in the inner medulla, primarily via sodium chloride and urea recycling.

Step 2: Transport in Henle's Loop and Vasa Recta
Sodium chloride transported out by the ascending limb of Henle's loop enters the descending limb of the vasa recta. As blood ascends towards the cortex through the ascending limb of the vasa recta, this sodium chloride is returned back to the medullary interstitium, preventing medullary solute depletion.

Step 3: Transport in Collecting Duct
Small amounts of urea enter the thin ascending limb of Henle's loop and are recycled back to the inner medullary interstitium through the collecting duct, preserving high hypertonicity.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Ascending limb of Henle's loop with transports sodium chloride that is exchanged with descending limb of vasa recta, Descending limb of vasa recta with takes up sodium chloride from medullary interstitium as blood flows downward, Ascending limb of vasa recta with returns sodium chloride back to the medullary interstitium, and Collecting duct with allows small amounts of urea into medullary interstitium to maintain osmolarity.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Transport processes during human urine formation

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological transport mechanisms in Column I with their appropriate functional descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Glomerular ultrafiltration I. Movement of water in initial segments and nitrogenous wastes along concentration gradients
B. Active tubular reabsorption II. Secretion of hydrogen ions, potassium ions, and ammonia to maintain acid-base balance
C. Passive tubular reabsorption III. Non-selective filtration of plasma except proteins across three layers driven by capillary pressure
D. Tubular secretion IV. Selective carrier-mediated uptake of glucose, amino acids, and sodium ions against gradients

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Urine formation relies on three integrated processes: non-selective glomerular ultrafiltration, selective active/passive tubular reabsorption, and active tubular secretion.

Step 2: Filtration Mechanics
Glomerular ultrafiltration is driven by glomerular capillary blood pressure filtering blood through the capillary endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte slit pores, allowing all plasma constituents except proteins into Bowman's space.

Step 3: Reabsorption and Secretion Pathways
Substances like glucose, amino acids, and sodium ions undergo active tubular reabsorption against concentration gradients, whereas water in early segments and nitrogenous wastes are reabsorbed passively down concentration gradients. Tubular secretion selectively moves hydrogen ions, potassium ions, and ammonia into the filtrate to maintain body fluid pH and electrolyte balance.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Glomerular ultrafiltration with non-selective filtration of plasma except proteins across three layers driven by capillary pressure, Active tubular reabsorption with selective carrier-mediated uptake of glucose, amino acids, and sodium ions against gradients, Passive tubular reabsorption with movement of water in initial segments and nitrogenous wastes along concentration gradients, and Tubular secretion with secretion of hydrogen ions, potassium ions, and ammonia to maintain acid-base balance.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Physiological values in human renal functioning

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological parameters in Column I with their standard normal values in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Glomerular filtration rate per day I. \(25\text{ to }30\text{ g}\)
B. Renal blood filtration per minute II. \(180\text{ litres}\)
C. Daily excretion of urea in adult human III. \(200\text{ mL}\)
D. Carbon dioxide eliminated by lungs per minute IV. \(1100\text{ to }1200\text{ mL}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Physiological Constants
Quantitative values defined in human physiology characterize standard filtration rates, blood throughput, and excretory elimination capacities.

Step 2: Renal Perfusion and Ultrafiltration Volumes
In a healthy adult, kidneys filter approximately \(1100\text{ to }1200\text{ mL}\) of blood per minute, which accounts for roughly one-fifth of cardiac output. The glomerular filtration rate is about \(125\text{ mL/min}\), which totals \(180\text{ litres}\) of filtrate formed per day.

Step 3: Excretory Turnover Values
Out of the filtered volume, about \(99\%\) is reabsorbed, resulting in \(1\text{ to }1.5\text{ litres}\) of urine containing an average of \(25\text{ to }30\text{ g}\) of urea excreted per day. Additionally, the lungs remove approximately \(200\text{ mL}\) of carbon dioxide each minute.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Glomerular filtration rate per day with \(180\text{ litres}\), Renal blood filtration per minute with \(1100\text{ to }1200\text{ mL}\), Daily excretion of urea in adult human with \(25\text{ to }30\text{ g}\), and Carbon dioxide eliminated by lungs per minute with \(200\text{ mL}\).
